author: Bill Maurer
title: Nobody should be surprised by the panic we are seeing when i
text:
Nobody should be surprised by the panic we are seeing when it comes to street analysts regarding Apple ( AAPL ) ahead of Thursday's earnings report. Not only is this a theme that seems to happen almost every quarter as earnings approach, but I started warning investors about the street turning on the iPhone X back in December. Over the last few days, we've finally seen a large adjustment to analyst estimates, which has taken down the stock as seen below. But is this panic really warranted?
( Source: Yahoo Finance) 
I cautioned investors that analysts would take down their estimates as earnings approached , and that scenario is playing out exactly as I figured it would. The biggest pillar of this week's panic is a report that Apple is cutting iPhone X production to 20 million units in the current quarter. You can read all about that as well as multiple analyst notes on the situation here . The chart below shows how estimates have accelerated downward recently, with still more than a day to go until Apple gives guidance for the March ending period.
( Source: Yahoo Finance analyst estimates page) 
The current figure still is a bit misleading, however, something you'd know if you read my recent earnings preview article or some of my past coverage. This is because the high estimate on the street calls for more than $83 billion in revenues for the fiscal Q2 period, which is either a really bullish analyst or perhaps a typo estimate that should have been included in Q1. Taking this estimate out completely drops the overall consensus by about $600 million, which will make Apple's guidance look a lot better.
I want to illustrate an example of how things could look for the March period, so to do that I looked at some of Apple's recent results. In the left box below, you can see the main highlights of Apple's March ending period from last year, and the right box shows the reported growth rates seen in the last quarterly report we have on record, which ended in September 2017.
( Source: Apple financial information page, Q2 and Q4 2017 reports) 
The iPad has been making a bit of a comeback, and Apple did raise prices last year in an effort to combat soaring memory prices, so even in a bear case let's think about a 5% revenue increase, which is still only one-third of what we saw in the September period. Likewise, we'll assume a 10% increase for Mac revenues, which will be helped by that super high end version . Services have been running around a 20% growth rate for most quarters (the 34% above was partially due to a one-time adjustment if you remember), so we'll throw that into the model. Other products also should do nicely thanks to the strength of the Apple Watch as well as nearly two months of initial HomePod sales, so I'll throw 20% in for a conservative growth rate there.
That gets me back to the iPhone, which sold over 50.76 million units last year. Let's assume absolutely no growth, but that 20 million units are the iPhone X we are hearing about. I'll model $1,050 as an average selling price for the blended X sales, along with a $630 ASP for the other 30 million or so units, which is a drop of roughly $25 over last year. Combining all of this gets me to a revenue number of about $62.8 billion for the March period.
That would be right in the middle of the predicted $62-$64 billion range for guidance from analyst Tony Sacconaghi, in a note issued on Tuesday. Again, however, some of those numbers seem fairly conservative. What if the iPad comes in with a 10% revenue growth rate, or the Mac comes in at 15%? What if services and other products grow more than I expected? I could easily add another billion or so to my base case. This also assumes that overall iPhone unit sales are flat. What if they grow even a couple of percent?
Finally, there is one other major elephant in the room that nobody seems to be discussing in all of this: The weaker US dollar. The chart below shows a roughly 10% decline in the dollar index over the past year, with some currencies showing even more strength against the greenback than that. When foreign results are translated into US dollars, a weaker dollar helps Apple. If you take half of a $62 billion quarter (last year's Q2 saw 60% of sales outside of the Americas) and improve it by even 5% overall to adjust for a weaker dollar, that's over a billion and a half dollars right there.
( Source: cnbc.com dollar index page) 
Here's the real question that investors have to ask themselves when looking at what Apple gives for guidance tomorrow. If you are a long-term investor, not someone just looking to make a quick buck, does it really matter if revenue guidance is for growth 19.1% ($63 billion) or 24.8% ($66 billion)? Does a few extra percentage points of growth in any one quarter really matter to whether or not you should hold Apple shares over the next 5-10 years? There are plenty of reasons to be positive on the future, like the massive capital return plan, lower tax rates, etc. Also, you have to take into consideration the pullback in Apple shares from $180 to $167 currently.
As we get closer to Apple's Thursday earnings report, there is a full blown panic when it comes to the tech giant. Analysts are racing to lower estimates thanks to potentially poor iPhone X sales, but are they ignoring the bigger picture? Even if Apple guidance is in the low to mid $60 billion range, we're still talking about a revenue growth rate of around or slightly above 20%, which is very strong for a company of this size. Apple shares have come well off their highs recently, so you're not paying an all-time high for the stock. Those looking at the bright future might actually consider this pullback as one to take advantage of. I really don't think this panic is fully warranted, but what do you think?
